original_question: Determine whether there exist a finitely generated free group F, a group Γ that is residually soluble but not free, and a homomorphism ψ: F -> Γ such that for every j >= 1 the induced map F/D^j(F) -> Γ/D^j(Γ) is an isomorphism, equivalently such that the induced map on true prosoluble completions PS(ψ): PS(F) -> PS(Γ) is an isomorphism.
target_in_paper: The unnumbered open problem in §7(C) asking whether there exist a finitely generated free group F, a residually soluble nonfree group Γ, and a homomorphism ψ: F → Γ inducing isomorphisms on all derived-series quotients, equivalently an isomorphism on true prosoluble completions.
correct_elements: Your draft is already extremely close to the paper’s exact formulation in §7(C). It correctly identifies the problem as an existence question, keeps the hypotheses narrow, uses the right objects (a finitely generated free group F, a residually soluble group Γ that is not free, and a homomorphism ψ: F → Γ), has the correct quantifier j ≥ 1, and includes the paper’s explicit equivalent formulation in terms of the induced map PS(ψ) on true prosoluble completions.
missing_details: To be fully stand-alone, define the derived series notation: for a discrete group G, D_0(G) = G and D_{j+1}(G) = [D_j(G), D_j(G)]. The paper writes D_j rather than D^j.
Define PS(G) as the true prosoluble completion of G, i.e. the procompletion with respect to all normal subgroups N ◁ G such that G/N is soluble.

If complete self-containment is desired, spell out that 'residually soluble' means every nontrivial element survives in some soluble quotient, equivalently that the canonical map G → PS(G) is injective.
Do not add extra hypotheses not present in the paper: in §7(C), Γ is not assumed finitely generated or finitely presented; only F is assumed finitely generated.

The equivalence between the quotient-by-derived-series formulation and the PS(ψ)-isomorphism formulation depends on §5(B)-(D), where PS(G) is identified with the procompletion coming from the derived-series quotients.
refined_question: Does there exist a finitely generated free group F, a residually soluble group Γ that is not free, and a homomorphism ψ: F → Γ such that, if D_0(G) = G and D_{j+1}(G) = [D_j(G), D_j(G)] denote the ordinary derived series of a group G, then for every j ≥ 1 the induced homomorphism F/D_j(F) → Γ/D_j(Γ) is an isomorphism?
equivalent_formulation: Equivalently, does there exist such F, Γ, and ψ for which the induced map on true prosoluble completions PS(ψ): PS(F) → PS(Γ) is an isomorphism, where PS(G) is the completion of G with respect to all normal subgroups having soluble quotient?
justification: The draft matches the paper’s exact target almost verbatim: the broader prosoluble analogue of Grothendieck’s problem is posed in the Introduction (§1, pp. 1-2); PS and the induced map PS(ψ) are set up functorially in §4(B)-(D) (pp. 4-5); the derived-series notation and the identification of PS(G) with the procompletion determined by the derived quotients are given in §5(B)-(D) (pp. 7-8); §7(B) records the analogous pronilpotent/parafree observation that motivates the comparison; and §7(C) then states exactly your existence question, including the equivalence with PS(ψ) being an isomorphism (pp. 11-12). The only substantive omissions in the draft are the definitions of D_j and PS, plus the fact that the paper does not impose any further finiteness assumptions on Γ.
